summary: A memo from SRI-ARC supporting Bob Braden's point in RFC 430 about site-dependent FTP parameters. To fetch part of a structured NLS file without changing FTP, the NIC planned to append a field such as ;x program to the pathname used in STOR and RETR. That field would name a program for the server to run.

plainLanguage.summary: A trick where special instructions are added onto a file's name so a server knows to do something extra without changing the main rules.

subtitle: A technique to add server-specific parameters to FTP file requests without changing the protocol.

tldr.problem: Some servers have complex file structures or features that FTP cannot express with standard pathname syntax. Adding new FTP commands requires protocol changes and breaks older clients.
tldr.mechanism: Append a special field to the FTP pathname, such as `;x program [/ parameters ]`, to tell the server to run a program on the file. For structured NLS files, parameters specify conversion algorithms, statement addresses, and view specifications.
tldr.outcome: This technique allows FTP servers to support site-specific functionality while remaining compatible with basic FTP clients.

facts.label: Approach
facts.value: Pathname encoding rather than protocol change

today: This RFC demonstrates an early approach to extending protocols via parameter encoding. Modern protocols typically use version negotiation and optional extension mechanisms instead.

sections.title: The FTP Parameter Problem
sections.content: FTP works well for copying simple files between computers, but it does not handle site-specific needs. SRI-ARC's NIC needed to let users fetch parts of an NLS tree-structured file from the network, translating them to sequential form. The problem: this required passing information through FTP without modifying the protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC had a special kind of file that FTP could not handle directly, so they invented a trick to make it work.

sections.title: Pathname Extension Syntax
sections.content:
The solution appends a field to standard TENEX filenames in the form `;x program [ / parameters ]`. This tells the server's FTP process to dispatch the named program with a pointer to the file being stored or retrieved, optionally passing additional parameters.

For NLS files, the program is named 'NLS' with parameters specifying the conversion algorithm (T:), statement address (S:), and view specifications (V:), each optional and separated by commas.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of just sending a filename, you add extra instructions in a special format that the server understands and acts on.

sections.title: Avoiding Protocol Changes
sections.content:
This design is elegant because it avoids modifying FTP itself. Old FTP clients continue to work, unaware of the extension field. The server's FTP process simply parses the pathname, recognizes the special format, and executes the appropriate program.

As the RFC notes, this approach generalizes beyond NLS files. Any server could define its own programs and parameter formats using the same syntax, allowing sites to add features without waiting for protocol updates.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular FTP clients ignore the extra instructions, so they keep working. Servers that understand the trick use the extra part to do special things.

references.text: Braden, R., "COMMENTS ON FILE TRANSFER PROTOCOL", RFC 430, February 1973.
